transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist here. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Doc. Well, I guess I'm here because I just feel like I'm always running hot. It's like I can't shut the motor off, honestly. And lately, that's actually been getting me into some trouble at the firehouse.

When you say you're always running hot and can't shut the motor off, have these feelings been pretty constant over time, or do they come and go in distinct periods where you feel much more energized or revved up than usual?

It's pretty constant, honestly. I wouldn't say it comes and goes in phases or anything like that. It's just... kind of my normal baseline. I don't really have periods where I suddenly feel way more revved up than usual. It's just always there. Like the idle is just set too high all the time, if that makes sense.
How far back does this feeling of running hot and not being able to shut your motor off go? Has it been like this since you were a kid, or did it start at some point in your adult life?

It's been like this since I was a kid, really. My mom says I was just like this back in grade school, too. I was always getting out of my seat, blurting out answers... losing my homework. She used to get notes sent home about my behavior all the time, even though the teachers would say I was bright enough to actually do the work. So, yeah, it's definitely not just an adult thing.
Besides losing your homework and blurting things out, do you find it hard to pay attention or concentrate on tasks? Like, do you get easily distracted or have trouble keeping your mind on one thing?

Yeah, definitely. It's really hard for me to keep my mind on one thing. Like, at work, I get distracted so easily. Just a radio chirp, somebody walking past the bay, or even just a random thought about a call from yesterday can completely knock me off what I’m doing. And once that happens, it takes me forever to actually get back on track with whatever I was supposed to be focusing on.

You mentioned getting out of your seat a lot as a kid and having trouble staying focused now. In your daily life right now, do you find yourself constantly fidgeting, tapping your feet, moving around in your seat, or having trouble sitting still even when you need to?

Yeah, pretty much constantly. Like, if I'm sitting in a meeting at the station, my leg is always bouncing. I'll be clicking a pen, shifting around in the chair, or... I don't know, just messing with whatever happens to be on the table in front of me. And most of the time, I'm doing it without even noticing it until I catch myself. It's just really hard for me to sit completely still.
You mentioned these things have been getting you into trouble at the firehouse lately. Can you tell me more about what kind of trouble that's been, and how it's affecting your work or relationships?

It's mostly that it's starting to cost me trust at the firehouse. I actually got pulled into a performance and safety meeting recently because of it. It's tough because... well, I was really hoping to move up into leadership, but right now it feels like that shot is slipping away. The crew just feels like they can't count on me to track all the details consistently. And in our line of work, if they can't trust you to stay on top of things, it's a real problem.

Besides what's happening at work, have these attention and fidgeting issues caused problems in other areas of your life — like in your relationships, school back in the day, or other activities outside of work?

Honestly, not that I can really think of. I mean, school was a long time ago when I got my associate's, and I don't remember it being a huge disaster back then. 

And as for relationships or just being at home... I don't know, I guess I just haven't noticed it causing major problems. Like, if I get distracted at the house and forget to finish a chore or I'm fidgeting on the couch, it's just not a life-or-death thing, you know? Nobody is really grading me on it. It's really just at the firehouse where the stakes are so high that it's become this serious issue. So yeah, outside of work, I don't really have much to report.

When you think back to your school years or even now in your personal life, have these attention and fidgeting issues ever caused you real problems — like affecting your grades, getting you into trouble, damaging relationships, or making it hard to do things you wanted to do?

Well, like I said, I don't really remember it being a huge disaster when I was getting my associate's. But... I guess if I think back further, to when I was a kid, my mom says I was pretty much exactly like this. 

She told me that back in grade school, I was always getting out of my seat during class. I'd just blurt out answers before the teacher even finished asking the question. And I was constantly losing my homework. She said I was always getting notes sent home from the teachers about my behavior, even though they all said I was bright enough to actually do the work. It was just the staying in my seat and keeping track of things that was the problem. So I guess it did cause some trouble back then.

You mentioned the attention and fidgeting issues are really affecting your job performance and career prospects at the firehouse. But thinking about your personal life overall — your relationships, hobbies, managing your home, or anything else you care about — would you say these symptoms actually get in the way of doing things that matter to you, or do they mostly just happen without really affecting how your personal life goes?

Honestly, I think they mostly just happen without really affecting things at home. Like I mentioned before, the stakes are just lower there. 

If I get sidetracked while I'm fixing something in the garage, or if I'm bouncing my leg while watching a movie, it doesn't really ruin my day or hurt my relationships. It doesn't stop me from doing the things I care about on my days off. My family and friends are pretty much used to it by now, I guess. So, yeah, it doesn't really get in the way of my personal life... it's really just the job where it's causing actual damage.

You've mentioned that these attention and fidgeting issues are really affecting your job performance and career prospects at the firehouse. But I want to make sure I understand the full picture: has there ever been a time in your life — whether in school, in past relationships, or in other areas — when these symptoms actually caused you real problems or got in the way of things that mattered to you?

Like I said, when I was a kid, yeah, it definitely caused real trouble at school. But as an adult, it really all comes back to the firehouse. That's what matters most to me, and it's... well, it's causing real damage there. 

It's gotten to the point where it's starting to cost me trust with the guys. I actually got pulled into a performance and safety meeting recently because of it. I've been working hard and wanting to move up, but now my shot at leadership feels like it's slipping away. The rest of the crew just feels like they can't count on me to track the details consistently, and in our line of work, that's a huge deal. So, yeah, even if it's not ruining my home life, it's definitely getting in the way of my career and the things I care about.

You mentioned your mom noticed these behaviors back in grade school — do you remember roughly what age you were when she first started seeing these things, like the getting out of your seat and losing your homework?

Well, from what she told me, it was pretty early on. She said I was like this back in grade school, so probably around seven or eight years old. That's when she really remembers the issues starting—you know, me always being out of my seat during class, blurting out the answers before the teacher finished, and just constantly losing my homework. She got a lot of notes sent home about my behavior, even though the teachers always said I was bright enough to do the work. It just started way back then.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with lifelong history of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity beginning in early childhood (grade school, age 7-8). Core ADHD symptoms include: difficulty sustaining attention (easily distracted at work), persistent fidgeting and restlessness (leg bouncing, pen clicking, constant movement), and impulsive behaviors (blurting out answers). Symptoms are pervasive across time and have caused functional impairment in multiple domains historically (school performance) and currently (occupational functioning with documented performance/safety meeting). While personal/social functioning remains relatively preserved, significant occupational impairment is present. Symptoms do not cluster into distinct manic or hypomanic episodes. Presentation is consistent with ADHD, Combined Type (F90.2) given evidence of both inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive symptoms, though F90.9 (ADHD, unspecified) is the provided candidate.
